notes: The catalogue's raspberry-pi-4 card only has the port GPIO_HEADER (plus USB, HDMI, Ethernet), so the individual pins GPIO4, GPIO17, GPIO27, GPIO10 and GND can't be addressed on it. lookup_part returned the same card. I replaced the Pi with a drafted type, raspberry-pi-4-gpio, which breaks out the 40-pin header as named pins (GPIOn, GND.1-8, 3V3.1-2, 5V.1-2) and adds AUDIO_JACK and USB_C_POWER. It is the same physical board, so the part count is unchanged.
All GND header pins are declared as one node and the two 3V3 and two 5V pins likewise. The GND lead uses GND.1 (physical pin 6, next to GPIO4's pin 7).

The tutorial doesn't give the exact wiring. It says each of four buttons goes to its own GPIO pin and uses the standard GPIO button wiring to GND. I used the example pins from the code: GPIO4 (drum), GPIO17 (cymbal), GPIO27 (snare), GPIO10 (bell). gpiozero Button uses the internal pull-up, so no external resistor is needed.

Each button straddles the breadboard centre gap: side 1 (1.l, 1.r) in the top half at columns c and c+2, side 2 (2.l, 2.r) in the bottom half. The GPIO jumper goes to the top (side 1) column. A pin-to-pin jumper takes the bottom (side 2) column to the bottom negative rail (bn).
The fifth pin-to-socket lead runs from the Pi GND to bn.1. bn is one rail strip, so bn.1, bn.2, bn.8, bn.13 and bn.18 are the same node.
Pin-to-socket leads: the female end (port a) goes on the Pi header pin and the male end (port b) goes into the breadboard.
Speakers or headphones plug into the Pi's 3.5mm audio jack. The headphones type is drafted because it isn't in the catalogue or on the approved shop sites.
Software steps (sample files, Thonny, pygame) are not physical parts, so they are not in the graph.
